a216.speaker: The Gambia Red Cross Society (GRCS)
a216.speech: Said the project aims to empower vulnerable communities to adapt to climate change through locally-led, integrated, and multi-sectoral approaches and also seeks to build sustained climate resilience at the community level and ensure transformational change across National Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies' institutional setups, programmes, and operations, making them climate-smart.

a216.speaker: Fabakary Kalleh, President of the Gambia Red Cross Society
a216.speech: In his welcome statement, said the project represents a significant milestone in their efforts to combat the adverse impacts of climate change in the Gambia: "Climate change is no longer a distant threat; it is a present and urgent challenge that demands immediate and concerted action. As a country, Gambia faces increased vulnerability to extreme weather events and shifting climatic patterns. If it's not flooding, then it's drought or other climate events that lead to damaging impacts. We need to act now to address some of the adaptation challenges." ; Said the project's target is to empower Gambian communities to lead the charge in adapting to the changing climate, ensuring that its responses are not only effective but sustainable and community-driven.

a216.speaker: Fabakary Kalleh, President of the Gambia Red Cross Society
a216.speech: While expressing gratitude to USAID, IFRC, stakeholders, and all their partners for both their financial and technical support, called on the Gambia government to continue playing a fundamental role in this initiative: "The government's support is crucial in creating an enabling environment for climate adaptation and resilience. This includes enacting supportive policies, providing necessary resources, and facilitating collaborations with various stakeholders. Together, we can create a more resilient and sustainable future for The Gambia."

a216.speaker: Muhammed B.S Jallow, Vice President of The Gambia
a216.speech: Delivering his launch statement, called on all Gambians to take action as he said climate change adaptation is not the responsibility of a few but the duty of all; assured the government's continuous support and said they will ensure that the national development plans are aligned with climate resilience and sustainability goals ; "The challenges posed by climate change are immense, but so too is our resolve. Today, as we launch this project, let us commit ourselves to taking bold and collective action. Let us work together to build a resilient and sustainable Gambia, where our communities can thrive despite the challenges of a changing climate." ; "The government of The Gambia recognizes the gravity of this situation. We are committed to taking decisive action to mitigate the impacts of climate change and to build resilience within our communities. However, government action alone is not enough. We need the collective effort of every Gambian, every community, and every sector, to rise to this challenge."

a216.speaker: Sharon L. Cromer, U.S. Ambassador to The Gambia
a216.speech: Assured her government's support to the fight against climate change: "We are committed to building the capacities of the Gambian communities to identify their challenges as well as the durable solutions to tackle climate change."

a237.speaker: Hamissa Mobetto, Tanzanian model and musician, now wife of Aziz Ki
a237.speech: "I got here after finding someone who loves me sincerely. Our souls are in harmony. I pray to God to guide us as we move forward with our plans."

a237.speaker: Aziz Ki, Burkinabè international footballer
a237.speech: Says he has found the woman of his dreams.

a408.speaker: Joe Biden, US President
a408.speech: Confirmed the deal, which involves a full and complete ceasefire, the withdrawal of Israeli forces from Gaza and the release of all the hostages held by Hamas ; says the first phase will allow Palestinians to return home to their neighbourhoods and let more humanitarian assistance into the Gaza Strip.

a408.speaker: Hamas-run health ministry (Gaza)
a408.speech: According to the Hamas-run health ministry, more than 46,000 Palestinians have been killed during the Israeli offensive on Gaza.

a408.speaker: Israel (government)
a408.speech: Says 94 hostages are still being held by Hamas, of whom 34 are presumed dead.

a574.speaker: Joyce Banda, former President of Malawi
a574.speech: In a recent exclusive interview hosted by Leah Malekano of Zodiak Broadcasting Station, she articulated her vision for Malawi and reminded Malawians that her government managed to ensure the availability of fuel, forex, and electricity within her first 100 days of being in power.

a600.speaker: UNAIDS
a600.speech: Has announced a dramatic price reduction for lenacapavir, a revolutionary HIV prevention drug, described as a watershed moment for global health; the announcement, made on Tuesday during the United Nations General Assembly, detailed two agreements slashing the cost of lenacapavir from USD 28,000 per patient per year to just USD 40.

a600.speaker: Winnie Byanyima, UNAIDS Executive Director
a600.speech: "This is a watershed moment. A price of USD 40 per person per year is a leap forward that will help unlock the revolutionary potential of long-acting HIV medicines."

a600.speaker: Winnie Byanyima, UNAIDS Executive Director
a600.speech: Noted that 1.3 million people were infected with HIV in 2024, far exceeding the 2025 target of 370,000.

a600.speaker: Winnie Byanyima, UNAIDS Executive Director
a600.speech: "UNITAID, Gates, CHAI, Wits RHI, Reddy, and Hetero have shown what is possible when companies prioritise equitable access to lifesaving medicines. Gilead must match this ambition by reducing its price for lenacapavir, being transparent on cost and pricing, expanding its generics licence to all low and middle-income countries, and enabling rapid access for more people in developing countries."

a600.speaker: PURPOSE 2 Trial, published in the New England Journal of Medicine
a600.speech: Found lenacapavir 96 to 100 per cent effective in preventing new HIV infections.

a600.speaker: UNAIDS (estimates)
a600.speech: Estimates that access for 20 million high-risk individuals, including men who have sex with men, sex workers, people who inject drugs, and young women and adolescent girls in sub-Saharan Africa, could significantly reduce infections and advance the goal of ending AIDS by 2030.

a600.speaker: Mduduzi Matsebula, Eswatini Health Minister
a600.speech: Welcomed the development, calling it timely for Eswatini: "We support the reduced pricing for this important commodity in the fight against HIV. This ensures the government can roll it out to all who need it. One of our vulnerabilities has been the persistently high rate of new infections among women of childbearing age, and this will help us turn this trend around."

a600.speaker: Dr Nondumiso Ginindza-Ncube, NERCHA Executive Director, and Ntsika Fakudze, NERCHA Board Chairman
a600.speech: Described the breakthrough as a game-changer for HIV prevention globally.

a600.speaker: Dr Nondumiso Ginindza-Ncube, NERCHA Executive Director
a600.speech: "As a country, we are looking forward to its launch during World AIDS Day on December 1 and have it ready for roll-out in January. Through UNAIDS, we have been promised about USD 660 000 (approximately E11.8 million) for a start, which is likely to benefit about 16 000 Emaswati" ; she added that PEPFAR has pledged further funding to support the programme ; noted that Eswatini has been prioritised for the drug, with rollout guidelines being developed with the World Health Organisation ; "Emaswati were either taking medications daily or monthly. Now, they will only need two injections per year at a lower cost per patient."

a657.speaker: Maano Mohamed Nur, principal of Abdalla Deerow Primary and Secondary School, Baidoa
a657.speech: Said the aim of establishing the school was "to provide education exclusively for girls who either lacked access to education or could not afford school fees."

a657.speaker: Maano Mohamed Nur, principal of Abdalla Deerow Primary and Secondary School, Baidoa
a657.speech: "The NGOs used to provide hygiene kits for the girls, learning materials like white chalks, and sanitation equipment." ; "But now, the NGOs are facing their own challenges, and we no longer receive the assistance we used to have."

a657.speaker: Maano Mohamed Nur, principal of Abdalla Deerow Primary and Secondary School, Baidoa
a657.speech: Raised early marriage as a major barrier for girls' education in Somalia: "When a girl is educated, she benefits herself, her family, her parents, and the entire country." ; "An educated girl represents an educated whole society. If a girl receives an education, she influences the entire community."

a657.speaker: Maano Mohamed Nur, principal of Abdalla Deerow Primary and Secondary School, Baidoa
a657.speech: Emphasized that it is never too late to return to school: "Even if a man once deceived you into early marriage, and now you have one or two children and have been left alone-you can still learn." ; "No one is too old to learn. Education is not about age; it's about your desire. Education is open and free for you. Come to Abdalla Deerow School-we welcome and support every girl who wants to learn."

a657.speaker: Jamila Abdiwahab, 16-year-old Form Three student at Abdalla Deerow School
a657.speech: "The challenge I face is that my school is far from our house." ; "When it rains, the road gets flooded and full of potholes, making it impassable. On those days, I cannot go to school."

a657.speaker: Anisa Ali Hassan, 14-year-old Form Three student at Abdalla Deerow School
a657.speech: "I don't like staying at home. Education is important. I would tell other girls that staying at home will not bring you anything. I urge you to go to school. Get an education for yourselves-it will help your family and your future."

a883.speaker: Nthomeng Majara, Deputy Prime Minister of Lesotho
a883.speech: Said the state of disaster would be in force until 30 June 2027.

a883.speaker: Official figures
a883.speech: According to official figures, unemployment in Lesotho stands at 30% but for young people the rate is almost 50%.

a883.speaker: Lesotho declaration under the Disaster Management Act
a883.speech: Allows the state to “take all necessary measures to… minimise the effects of disasters” among others.

a883.speaker: Officials in Lesotho
a883.speech: Say the move will allow the government to quickly divert funds to programmes aimed at getting young people into work and helping the economy to recover.

a883.speaker: AFP report
a883.speech: According to an AFP report, the textile-dependent economy was already grappling with sky-high unemployment, especially among young people, before Trump slashed aid and raised trade barriers ; the government has warned it could lose up to 40,000 jobs if Agoa is not renewed at the end of September.

a883.speaker: US government
a883.speech: According to the US government, the two countries traded goods worth $240m (£187m) in 2024, mostly exports from Lesotho to the US, in particular textiles and clothing.

a883.speaker: Mokhethi Shelile, Lesotho’s Trade Minister
a883.speech: Told South African business news site Moneyweb last month that US buyers were “not placing orders because they don’t understand what is going to happen.”

a883.speaker: Sam Matekane, Prime Minister of Lesotho
a883.speech: Said around 700,000 Basotho were facing extreme hunger, worsened by prolonged drought.

a991.speaker: Felix Okech, the WFP’s head of refugee operations in Kenya (United Nations official)
a991.speech: Told the BBC that hundreds of thousands of people are "slowly starving" in Kenyan refugee camps after US funding cuts reduced food rations to their lowest ever levels: "If we have a protracted situation where this is what we can manage, then basically we have a slowly starving population." ; "It is a really dire situation" ; "We do have some signals from some one or two donors about support with that cash component. But remember, the very kind and generous US has been providing over 70% - so if you're still missing 70%… those prospects are not good."

a991.speaker: World Food Programme (WFP)
a991.speech: Says that as a result of the US aid cuts, the agency has had to slash the refugees’ rations to 30% of the minimum recommended amount a person should eat to stay healthy.

a991.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a991.speech: Announced sweeping cuts to US foreign aid programmes earlier this year, as part of his "America First" policy.

a991.speaker: A medic at Amusait Hospital, Kakuma camp (unnamed)
a991.speech: Tells the BBC that the wrinkled and peeling skin of baby Hellen is the result of malnutrition.

a991.speaker: Agnes Awila, refugee from northern Uganda
a991.speech: "The food is not enough, my children eat only once a day. If there's no food what do you feed them?"

a991.speaker: Mukuniwa Bililo Mami, refugee from South Kivu, mother of two
a991.speech: "I am grateful to receive this little [food] but it is not enough." Says the refugees used to "eat well" - three meals a day - but now that rations are at 30% of their usual amount, the food she has been given is not enough to last one month, let alone the two that she has been asked to stretch it for.

a991.speaker: Badaba Ibrahim, refugee trader from the Nuba Mountains in Sudan
a991.speech: Says his customers, now unable to purchase food, at times camp at his shop all day, begging for help: "They will tell you, 'My children have not eaten for a full day.'"

a991.speaker: Agnes Livio, refugee from South Sudan
a991.speech: "We used to get porridge for breakfast but not anymore. So, the children have to wait until the afternoon to have their first meal."

a999.speaker: Yinager Dessie (PhD), Governor of the National Bank of Ethiopia
a999.speech: Decided to slash reserve requirements for the commercial banks by half, ordered the banks to submit weekly and monthly reports on their deposits and reserve balances to the central bank’s supervision directorate, and directed banks to keep liquid assets of at least 15pc of net liabilities; he hopes cutting the reserve requirement by half would ease the banking industry’s liquidity problem.

a999.speaker: Ahmed Shide, Finance Minister
a999.speech: Told Parliamentarians two weeks ago that although deposit mobilisation efforts have improved, the volume of Birr outside the banks is growing, with an estimated 133.6 billion Br circulating outside the banking system by the end of the last financial year.

a999.speaker: Solomon Desta, vice governor of the central bank in charge of supervising financial institutions
a999.speech: Told Fortune: “There is no liquidity crunch in the banking system.”

a999.speaker: Solomon Desta, vice governor of the central bank in charge of supervising financial institutions
a999.speech: On the purpose of the reserve cut: “The intent of reducing the reserve requirement is to boost banks’ ability and reach businesses affected by the conflict.”

a999.speaker: Abdulmenan Mohammed, accounts manager at the London-based Portbello Group Ltd
a999.speech: Sees no other reason to force the central bank to halve the reserve requirement: “There’s a severe liquidity problem in the banking industry due to a significant expansion of credits.”

a999.speaker: Industry players and bank executives
a999.speech: Say a shortage of deposits over the past half-year has made it challenging to process loan applications that involve large projects, and that although liquidity issues are not new to the industry, the effects are more severe this time, worsened by growing demand for credit from war-affected areas.

a999.speaker: Desalege Tolera, chief credit analyst at Awash Bank
a999.speech: “We’ve been facing a liquidity crunch recently. The latest move will improve our position for credit disbursement.”

a999.speaker: Genene Ruga, president of Nib International Bank
a999.speech: Argues the loan-to-deposit ratio does not necessarily reflect the real picture as it fluctuates often, disclosing that his Bank’s ratio stood at 84pc in March but dropped four percentage points since; however, he agrees that the central bank’s latest decision will help ease liquidity problems: "We're willing to disburse loans to conflict-stricken areas as long as applicants present feasible proposals.”

a999.speaker: Arega Shumite (PhD), senior researcher at the Ethiopian Economics Association
a999.speech: Cautions: "Inflation will worsen unless the newly-injected money is pulled out of the economy quickly."

a1009.speaker: Mali's law of 12 November 2015 establishing measures to promote gender in access to appointed and elected office
a1009.speech: It grants women a quota of at least 30% for appointments "in the institutions of the Republic or in the various categories of public services in Mali by decree, order or decision"; the same applies at the electoral level, "including the conditions under which the admissibility of a candidate list is subject to a maximum proportion of 70% of women or men".

a1009.speaker: UN Women report
a1009.speech: A UN Women report recalls that women's rights regressed in one country out of four in 2024.

a1009.speaker: "Beijing +30" evaluation documents
a1009.speech: According to various "Beijing +30" evaluation documents, gender-based violence remains a global scourge: a woman or girl is killed every 10 minutes by a partner or a member of her own family; one woman in three still suffers physical or sexual violence in the course of her life; in 54% of countries the legal definition of rape is still not based on the principle of free and informed consent; and in 2023, 612 million women lived close to a war zone, a figure up 50% in a decade.

a1009.speaker: UN Women
a1009.speech: To preserve gains and accelerate change in terms of protection and promotion, UN Women recommends six priority areas for the future: a digital revolution for all women and girls ensuring equal access to technology and safety online; eliminating poverty by investing in comprehensive social protection, universal health coverage, education and strong care services; that countries adopt and implement "legislation to end violence against women and girls, in all its forms"; strengthening temporary special measures such as gender quotas; "fully funding national plans on women, peace and security and on gender-responsive humanitarian aid"; and climate justice giving priority to the rights of women and girls, placing their leadership and knowledge at the centre of interventions and ensuring they benefit from the creation of green jobs.

a1060.speaker: Famine Early Warning Systems Network (Fewsnet), USAID's food security arm
a1060.speech: says the country's macroeconomic environment will likely remain volatile despite some relative stability witnessed at the end of 2022 ; In its latest food security outlook covering the February to September 2023 period, Fewsnet said the local currency...

a1231.speaker: Professor Riziki Shemdoe, Permanent Secretary, Ministry of Livestock and Fisheries of Tanzania
a1231.speech: called on livestock professionals in the country to be at the forefront of preventing the spread of livestock diseases to humans in order to help the Government avoid spending large sums of money treating preventable diseases; said preventing animal diseases from passing to humans is easier than treatment, which requires a lot of money and time ; “This training is very important for livestock professionals; treating livestock diseases in humans costs us far more money than tackling these diseases early. It is important to be at the forefront of preventing these diseases from passing to humans; by doing so we will have helped save a great deal of Government money that would have been spent on treatment.”

a1231.speaker: Professor Riziki Shemdoe, Permanent Secretary, Ministry of Livestock and Fisheries of Tanzania
a1231.speech: urged the professionals to use the training they received to vaccinate livestock so that Tanzania can continue to grow its international meat market, as there is already a country looking into the possibility of importing 54,000 tonnes of meat from the country.

a1231.speaker: Dr Rogath Kishimba, Coordinator of Epidemiology and Laboratory Management Training, Ministry of Health of Tanzania
a1231.speech: said the cost of livestock vaccination is small, but when a disease passes from an animal to a human the cost of treatment is high; giving the example of rabies, said a dog is vaccinated for Sh2,000, but a person bitten by a dog with the disease must receive four vaccine doses costing between Sh30,000 and Sh60,000 per dose.

a1231.speaker: Dr Rogath Kishimba, Coordinator of Epidemiology and Laboratory Management Training, Ministry of Health of Tanzania
a1231.speech: said that when a person contracts rabies and begins to show symptoms, the chance of recovery is small: “If you have 100 patients, on average only two can recover, or none at all recover; that is why we stress the importance of control - when it is in animals it is cheaper to treat and prevent.”

a1231.speaker: Dr Benezeth Lutege, Director of veterinary services, Ministry of Livestock and Fisheries of Tanzania
a1231.speech: said that in order to increase better availability of vaccines the Government has removed tax on livestock vaccines imported from abroad: “Vaccines and veterinary medicines in the country are imported free of tax, so we expect vaccine costs to be lower. Also, we have a dog vaccine we expect to produce and it is at various stages of production, and possibly by 2030 we will have begun production; we have also prepared a strategy to eliminate rabies from 2024 to 2028 and we have submitted it to the World Organisation for Animal Health.”

a1231.speaker: Innocent Mrope, livestock expert from Masasi
a1231.speech: said that among 300 people aged 18 and above surveyed in 15 villages in the district, 54.6 percent have no understanding of rabies and 32.3 percent had a negative attitude about the problem; said it is important that the district focuses on providing education to citizens about rabies because only 14 percent have a positive attitude about the disease, and most of them, when they face a problem related to the disease, do not believe in recovering through treatment or in vaccinating their dogs.

a1231.speaker: Mosses Ole Neselle, FAO Programme Coordinator
a1231.speech: said the livestock professionals enabled by the training number 30 - 20 from mainland Tanzania and 10 from Zanzibar; said the training is important because animal diseases endanger world food security and undermine countries’ economies.

a1231.speaker: World Organisation for Animal Health
a1231.speech: according to it, more than 70 percent of diseases occurring in the world come from animals to humans.

a1231.speaker: United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
a1231.speech: according to it, there are more than 200 diseases associated with transmission from animals to humans, meaning that 6 out of 10 infectious diseases that affect people are spread by animals, including domestic animals.

a1231.speaker: National Library of Medicine website (United States)
a1231.speech: shows that for diseases passing from animals to humans, 2.5 billion cases have been reported with 2.7 million deaths witnessed.

a1378.speaker: African Union Commission
a1378.speech: Says it is dismayed by the US government's decision to withdraw from the World Health Organisation (WHO).

a1378.speaker: Nicolas Maduro, President of Venezuela
a1378.speech: In his congratulatory message, wished the President-Elect, Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah, the greatest of success.

a1378.speaker: Moussa Faki Mahamat, Chairperson of the African Union Commission
a1378.speech: Visited Casa Rosalia to offer his condolences to former First Lady Monica Geingos and the children.

a1378.speaker: Moussa Faki Mahamat, Chairperson of the African Union Commission
a1378.speech: Says Africa must create wealth amongst its people as a tool to curb foreign aid and stimulate peace ; says the need to embrace African ideas on issues facing the continent is also critical to attaining transformation across all spheres of life.

a1378.speaker: Hage Geingob, President of Namibia
a1378.speech: Is concerned about the reversal of democratic processes in some African countries, more than 50 years after the continent rid itself of colonialism.

a1445.speaker: Embassy of the United States of America in Mozambique (press release)
a1445.speech: According to a press release from the US Embassy in Mozambique, the critical funding will help meet the urgent needs of affected populations in Cabo Delgado province, with a focus on shelter, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH); one of the grants will be implemented by the Adventist Development and Relief Agency (ADRA) and the other rapid response actions by CARE International; other USAID humanitarian partners are mobilising existing resources to respond to immediate needs; initial reports indicate that the greatest human and material losses occurred in the south of Cabo Delgado province and surrounding areas; assessments are under way to determine the full impact of the disaster, and the US Government will continue to work closely with the National Institute for Disaster Risk Management and Reduction to coordinate the cyclone response.

a1445.speaker: Peter H. Vrooman, United States Ambassador to Mozambique
a1445.speech: stressed the importance of rapid action to help those affected by Cyclone Chido: "The United States Government recognises the enormous challenges faced by the affected people and wants to reaffirm our solidarity. Our assistance will provide vital help to the people most impacted by the cyclone, helping to alleviate human suffering and to support recovery efforts," said Ambassador Vrooman, quoted in the same press release.

a1606.speaker: International Monetary Fund (IMF)
a1606.speech: Has endorsed the liberalisation of the operations of the Electricity Company of Ghana (ECG), the State-owned electricity distributor, for private sector participation; is of the view that private sector participation would attract the much-needed investment and technical expertise to address legacy debts, making the energy sector financially sustainable.

a1606.speaker: IMF July country report on the fourth review of Ghana's US$3 billion Extended Credit Facility (ECF) arrangement
a1606.speech: Identified the energy sector as a major source of fiscal risk; according to the Fund, in the absence of any policy action, the annual energy sector shortfall is estimated to reach US$2.2 billion in 2025, reflecting ECG's large commercial and technical losses and slow electricity tariff adjustment in the face of exchange rate fluctuations and higher power generation costs, notably due to reliance on costly liquid fuels ; the report indicated that "some IPPs received less than expected, as fuel payments and the addition of an IPP diluted Cash Waterfall Mechanism distributions" and noted significant deviations between ECG's validated and declared collections (GHS5.3 billion) and between CWM allocations and actual payments (GHS3.9 billion).

a1606.speaker: IMF staff appraisal on the ECF programme
a1606.speech: "Staff welcomes the cabinet decision to open the electricity company's operations to the private sector, and the efforts made towards the energy sector's financial sustainability -including resuming the quarterly electricity tariff increases."

a1606.speaker: International Monetary Fund (IMF)
a1606.speech: Observed progress in reducing the energy sector challenges including the 14.75 per cent increase in electricity tariffs in April 2025 by the Public Utilities Regulatory Commission (PURC) and somewhat improved compliance with the Cash Waterfall Mechanism in 2025; recommended a full and consistent implementation of the Cash Waterfall Mechanism, ensuring regular payments to Independent Power Producers (IPPs) and fuel suppliers, addressing legacy arrears, and improving transparency, governance and accountability; urged the Government to accelerate the implementation of the Energy Sector Recovery Programme measures, including conducting a multi-year tariff assessment by end-September 2025, enhance revenue collection and limit arrears accumulation.

a1606.speaker: Nana Amoasi VII, Executive Director, Institute for Energy Security
a1606.speech: Said in an earlier interview with the Ghana News Agency that privatisation could bring in expertise, investment, and efficiency improvements that are needed to address infrastructure challenges and improve service delivery in the power sector; referring to the 2019 failed agreement with Power Distribution Services (PDS), he called for a well-designed, transparent, and best practices approach to avoid the pitfalls experienced in the past deal.

a1606.speaker: Alice Albright, Chief Executive Officer of the Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC)
a1606.speech: Stated on Thursday, May 9, 2024, that the Corporation had no immediate plans, but remained open to working with Ghana for long-term sustainability of related infrastructure and financial recovery in the energy sector.

a1673.speaker: Jeune Afrique (investigation, "Comment la Russie conquiert le Sahel, de base en base")
a1673.speech: Reveals the extension of Russian influence in Africa. From Libya, where it has redeployed part of its troops initially stationed in Syria, the Russian army and its African arm, the Africa Corps, are strengthening their presence towards the south. Through testimonies and satellite images, the newspaper highlights the Russian war and equipment effort in southern Libya and in Chad.

a1673.speaker: L'Essor (Mali)
a1673.speech: Reports the meeting between the president of the transition, Assimi Goita, and the Malian diplomatic corps.

a1673.speaker: General Assimi Goita, President of Mali's transition
a1673.speech: "Respect for our sovereignty and our strategic choices is at the heart of our public action," stressed the general, reaffirming his commitment to continuing the momentum of the transition within the framework of respectful and mutually beneficial cooperation with the Sahelian country's friendly countries and partners.

a1673.speaker: Financial Afrik
a1673.speech: Indicates that neighbouring Burkina is currently seeking a technical and financial partner. The expanding West African dairy market is attracting growing interest from European dairy companies. However, the newspaper warns about the growing presence of milk re-fattened with vegetable oil, a product depleted in nutrients, which exposes consumers to an increased risk of malnutrition in this other Sahel country.

a1673.speaker: Bénin Web TV
a1673.speech: Reports that Ghana is seeking more than 150 million dollars after the suspension of aid from USAID, the American development agency. Ghana's president, John Mahama, has asked the Ministry of Finance to urgently find 156 million dollars to fill the gap linked to the freezing of aid by the United States.

a1673.speaker: Felix Kwakye Ofosu, spokesperson for the Ghanaian presidency
a1673.speech: Specified that Ghana's president, John Mahama, has asked the Ministry of Finance to urgently find 156 million dollars to fill the deficit linked to the freezing of aid by the United States.

a1673.speaker: Le Soleil (Senegal)
a1673.speech: Announces that the Autonomous Port of Dakar is seeking to regain a position lost to its sub-regional competitors, as part of a repositioning plan launched by its new managing director, Waly Diouf Bodiang. Losing momentum, the port is aiming for annual turnover of 200 billion FCFA, against 70 billion currently.

a1673.speaker: Sud Quotidien (Senegal)
a1673.speech: Mentions progress for Senegal, a "slight improvement" in the latest ranking of the Corruption Perceptions Index (CPI) for 2024. The country gains two points compared to 2023, reaching a score of 45 out of 100, but remains in the red zone, according to the newspaper.

a1673.speaker: Le Soleil (Senegal)
a1673.speech: Evokes the tragic death of the student Matar Diagne at Gaston Berger University in Saint-Louis (north). The young man left behind "a body, a letter and questions", headlines the national daily.

a1673.speaker: L'As (Senegal)
a1673.speech: Insists on the "deeply moving letter" left by Matar Diagne, in which he expressed his preference for dying with dignity rather than living in dishonour.

a1673.speaker: Public prosecutor of Saint-Louis
a1673.speech: Announced the opening of an investigation into this case.

a1683.speaker: International Criminal Court (ICC) (press release)
a1683.speech: Issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his former defence minister, Yoav Gallant, "for crimes against humanity and war crimes committed from at least 8 October 2023 until at least 20 May 2024". ; Among the war crimes charges against Netanyahu and Gallant are that "both individuals intentionally and knowingly deprived the civilian population in Gaza of objects indispensable to their survival, including food, water, and medicine and medical supplies, as well as fuel and electricity, from at least 8 October 2023 to 20 May 2024". ; The ICC has "found reasonable grounds to believe" that both Netanyahu and Gallant "each bear criminal responsibility as civilian superiors for the war crime of intentionally directing an attack against the civilian population".

a1683.speaker: International Criminal Court (ICC)
a1683.speech: Stopped short of calling Israel out on genocide, instead specifying that the court "could not determine that all elements of the crime against humanity of extermination were met".

a1683.speaker: United Nations committee
a1683.speech: Recently found Israel's methods of warfare in the Gaza Strip to be "consistent with genocide".

a1683.speaker: Israel (Israeli establishment position)
a1683.speech: In the eyes of Israel, the ICC decision constitutes a horrifying display of anti-Semitism and even support for "terror".

a1683.speaker: Fatou Bensouda, then-ICC prosecutor (2019 ICC announcement)
a1683.speech: The court announced in 2019, after nearly five years of "preliminary investigation", that then-prosecutor Fatou Bensouda was "satisfied" that there was a "reasonable basis to initiate an investigation into the situation in Palestine", having established that there was a "reasonable basis to believe that war crimes have been or are being committed in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, and the Gaza Strip".

a1725.speaker: Nikolay Azarov, former Ukrainian Prime Minister
a1725.speech: Recently said that Zelensky would certainly resign from his post and leave Ukraine, given his loss of political power and popular support, as well as Ukraine's absolutely catastrophic situation on the battlefield; according to Mr Azarov, Zelensky has no future in Ukraine.

a1725.speaker: Nikolay Azarov, former Ukrainian Prime Minister (Telegram channel)
a1725.speech: Said on his Telegram channel that Mr Zelensky would not stay in power much longer and also suggested that the "decision" to remove him from office had already been taken, not in Kyiv, which is merely a proxy, but in the United States; he believes Washington has already given the green light for Zelensky's replacement and that it is only a matter of time before the change takes place officially.

a1725.speaker: Nikolay Azarov, former Ukrainian Prime Minister
a1725.speech: On European support: made it clear that he did not believe in the effectiveness of European support; although the EU and the United Kingdom continue to support Zelensky unconditionally, this aid, according to Azarov, is insufficient to ensure the continuity of Zelensky's government in the long term.

a1725.speaker: Nikolay Azarov, former Ukrainian Prime Minister
a1725.speech: On Zelensky's exit: believes Zelensky will come under extreme pressure and will have no choice but to resign quickly, that he will try to seek the help and protection of certain units of the local army – mainly special forces – before resigning, but that his requests will be refused because of the military's dissatisfaction with his government: "I do not think Zelensky will stay in Ukraine after that (...) He will ask for protection, most likely from the special forces, but they will not make such sacrifices for him. The options for his future may vary (...) [But there is] a serious sign that the process of removing Zelensky has begun."

a2031.speaker: Afghan authorities
a2031.speech: Said on Monday that one of Afghanistan's worst earthquakes killed more than 800 people and injured at least 2,800; they added that casualties could rise as rescue teams access more isolated locations, that the quake razed three villages in Kunar with substantial damage in many others, and that at least 610 people were killed in Kunar with 12 dead in Nangarhar.

a2031.speaker: Sharafat Zaman, spokesperson for the health ministry in Kabul
a2031.speech: Called for international aid to tackle the devastation wrought by the quake. "We need it because here lots of people lost their lives and houses," he told Reuters.

a2031.speaker: Zabihullah Mujahid, administration spokesman
a2031.speech: Said the quake killed 812 people in the eastern provinces of Kunar and Nangarhar.

a2031.speaker: Ziaul Haq Mohammadi, student at Al-Falah University in Jalalabad
a2031.speech: Said he tried to stand up but was knocked over by the power of the tremor. "We spent the whole night in fear and anxiety because at any moment another earthquake could happen."

a2031.speaker: Kate Carey, officer at the U.N. Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (UNOCHA)
a2031.speech: "The area of the earthquake was affected by heavy rain in the last 24-48 hours as well, so the risk of landslides and rock slides is also quite significant – that is why many of the roads are impassable," she told Reuters ; said rescue teams and authorities are trying to dispose of animal carcasses quickly so as to minimise the risk of contamination to water resources.

a2031.speaker: Abdul Maten Qanee, health ministry spokesperson
a2031.speech: "All our … teams have been mobilised to accelerate assistance, so that comprehensive and full support can be provided," citing efforts in areas from security to food and health.

a2031.speaker: Afghan defence ministry (statement)
a2031.speech: Said in a statement that military rescue teams fanned out across the region, with 40 flights carrying away 420 wounded and dead.

a2031.speaker: Diplomats and aid officials
a2031.speech: Say crises elsewhere in the world, along with donor frustration over the Taliban's policies towards women, including curbs on those who are aid workers, have spurred the cuts in funding.

a2031.speaker: Humanitarian agencies
a2031.speech: Say they are fighting a forgotten crisis in Afghanistan.

a2031.speaker: United Nations (estimate)
a2031.speech: Estimates more than half the population of Afghanistan is in urgent need of humanitarian aid.

a2031.speaker: Spokesperson of Afghanistan's foreign office
a2031.speech: "So far, no foreign governments have reached out to provide support for rescue or relief work," said on Monday.

a2031.speaker: Spokesperson for China's foreign ministry
a2031.speech: Said China was ready to provide disaster relief assistance "according to Afghanistan's needs and within its capacity".

a2031.speaker: Subrahmanyam Jaishankar, Foreign Minister of India
a2031.speech: Said India had delivered 1,000 family tents to Kabul and was moving 15 tonnes of food material to Kunar, with more relief material to be sent from India starting Tuesday.

a2031.speaker: Antonio Guterres, U.N. Secretary General
a2031.speech: Said its mission in Afghanistan was preparing to help those in areas devastated by the quake.

a2386.speaker: Nasser Bourita, Moroccan Minister of Foreign Affairs, African Cooperation and Moroccans Residing Abroad
a2386.speech: Criticised the verbal attacks targeting the Secretary-General of the United Nations and foreign heads of state ; finally stressed that Morocco disapproves of the aggressions that target figures working for peaceful solutions.

a2386.speaker: Nasser Bourita, Moroccan Minister of Foreign Affairs, African Cooperation and Moroccans Residing Abroad
a2386.speech: Reiterated on Tuesday in Rabat the fundamental principles of Morocco’s position regarding the conflict in the Middle East, as defined by King Mohammed VI, Chairman of the Al-Quds Committee: “Morocco’s position is very clear and has been expressed on several occasions,” he declared at a press briefing following his talks with the president of the regional government of the Canary Islands, Fernando Clavijo; he recalled that the Kingdom is calling for going beyond crisis management in order to establish the foundations of a lasting solution ; reaffirmed Morocco’s commitment to a two-State solution, with the creation of an independent Palestinian State within the June 1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital: “It is essential that constructive actors take back the initiative so that the region is no longer held hostage by the extremists of both camps,” he insisted.

a2386.speaker: Nasser Bourita, Moroccan Minister of Foreign Affairs, African Cooperation and Moroccans Residing Abroad
a2386.speech: Called for international mobilisation to compel the United Nations to fully assume its responsibilities and to put an end to the attacks against the Palestinian people; denounced the violence targeting schools and hospitals as well as Palestinian women and children, while condemning the restrictions imposed on access to humanitarian aid, describing these acts as a policy of “starvation” of the population.

a2386.speaker: Benjamin Netanyahu, Israeli Prime Minister
a2386.speech: Facing Antonio Guterres, denounced “the UN’s anti-Israeli bias”; at the 79th session of the United Nations in New York he challenged Antonio Guterres and the international organisation, calling for a change in their approach towards Israel: “While positive changes are taking place in the world and in the Middle East, it is incomprehensible that the United Nations maintains a systematically hostile attitude,” he declared ; He urged the UN to condemn what he called “Iranian perversion” and Palestinian terrorist actions against innocent civilians, while asking the institution to put an end to its recurrent criticism of Israel.

a2403.speaker: Government of Zanzibar
a2403.speech: Said the sweeping programme of modernising and expanding its ports will unlock unprecedented opportunities in shipping, business, tourism and regional connectivity.

a2403.speaker: Dr Khalid Salum Mohamed, Minister for Infrastructure, Communication and Transport
a2403.speech: Said preparations are well underway to overhaul key ports on Unguja and Pemba islands, including new or upgraded facilities at Kizimkazi, Maruhubi, Mangapwani, Shumba, Wete and Mkoani, which he said will restore Zanzibar’s historic role as a gateway for Indian Ocean trade. “We are determined to move forward in the port sector and compete at the highest level,” he told journalists, noting that different ports will be tailored for specialised activities such as fishing, oil handling and passenger services.

a2403.speaker: Akif Ali Khamis, Zanzibar Ports Corporation (ZPC) Director General
a2403.speech: Said the government has embarked on transformative port reforms that will allow both domestic and international shipping lines to dock directly in Zanzibar, cutting costs and boosting trade. “These new facilities are being built to modern standards, with capacity for large cargo and passenger vessels and fitted with advanced handling equipment.” He singled out Mangapwani Port as the designated international trade gateway. “By 2027, all passenger services from Malindi will be relocated to the state-of-the-art Maruhubi terminal.”

a2403.speaker: Akif Ali Khamis, Zanzibar Ports Corporation (ZPC) Director General
a2403.speech: Said port revenues have grown from 27bn/- annually before Dr Mwinyi’s presidency to an average of 33bn/-, with collections reaching 36bn/- in 2024/25. “At Malindi Port alone, monthly income has more than doubled from 360m/- to over 800m/-, with projections to surpass 1bn/-.” ; “With the completion of Mkoani, Fumba and Mangapwani projects, we expect revenues to exceed 42bn/- annually within the next two years.” ; “Thirty years from now, Zanzibar’s ports will be fully modern, competitive and independent. This is the backbone of our economy and the key to placing Zanzibar firmly back on the global trade map.”

a2403.speaker: Ahmed Suleiman, Customs Chief Secretary
a2403.speech: Added that the government’s long-term vision is to ensure every region of Zanzibar has a modern port, strengthening services and expanding national revenue.

a2403.speaker: Officials (Zanzibar)
a2403.speech: Say the sweeping port transformation will be one of President Mwinyi’s defining legacies, setting Zanzibar on a path to self-reliance and prosperity for decades to come.

a2432.speaker: Pankaj Bedi, Chairman of apparel company United Aryan and Kenya Association of Manufacturers board member
a2432.speech: Told Reuters that African manufacturers are lobbying U.S. Congress to grant a last-ditch extension of one or two years to the duty-free AGOA trade programme due to expire at the end of September; said delegations from Kenya and four other AGOA beneficiaries visited Washington last week to push for the temporary extension; said the delegation of private investors and government officials had more than 30 engagements last week, including with members of Congress and their aides; said there was universal support from the Congressional Republicans and Democrats they met, including staffers for House Speaker Mike Johnson, to renew AGOA; but said it remained unclear whether Congress could find a piece of legislation in the next two weeks to which a renewal could be attached.

a2432.speaker: Pankaj Bedi, Chairman of United Aryan
a2432.speech: “It’s like a house of cards that will collapse,” predicting mass layoffs across the textiles sector if AGOA is not renewed ; said that if AGOA ends, the U.S. would become even more heavily dependent on Asian manufacturers: “If this is taken away, by default, the business is going to go back to China.”

a2432.speaker: The White House and the offices of the United States Trade Representative and Speaker Mike Johnson
a2432.speech: Did not respond immediately to requests for comment; the White House has not said publicly whether it supports an extension.

a2464.speaker: Amb. Linda Thomas-Greenfield, US Representative to the United Nations
a2464.speech: Said the funding will enable UN and nongovernmental partners to provide critical assistance to those affected by the ongoing conflict across Sudan and neighboring refugee receiving countries ; She highlighted the dire humanitarian suffering caused by the war in Sudan and called on the warring military factions to agree to a humanitarian ceasefire ; "More than 25 million Sudanese face acute hunger. Many are in famine…and some 11 million have fled their homes in what has become the worst humanitarian crisis on the planet" ; "We must compel the warring parties to accept humanitarian pauses in El Fasher, Khartoum, and other highly vulnerable areas, eliminate barriers to humanitarian access along all routes, and put down their weapons and come to the negotiating table."

a2464.speaker: US Embassy in Juba (press statement)
a2464.speech: The donation brings the total amount in US assistance to support people who fled the Sudan conflict to South Sudan to $105 million in the fiscal year 2024, according to a press statement from the US Embassy in Juba ; "We again urge South Sudan's transitional government to contribute more financial resources to humanitarian response as well as other public services, and to reduce the costs and risks faced by those seeking to help the South Sudanese people."

a2536.speaker: Ahmed Fahmy, spokesman for the Egyptian presidency (statement)
a2536.speech: "Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sissi and US President Joe Biden agreed on the delivery of humanitarian aid to the Gaza Strip through the Rafah crossing on a lasting basis," the presidency spokesman stressed in a statement, without specifying a concrete date.

a2536.speaker: Sameh Shoukry, Egyptian Minister of Foreign Affairs
a2536.speech: Revealed to the Al-Arabiya station that the delivery of aid will be supervised by the UN ; Asked whether foreigners and dual nationals wishing to leave would be allowed to cross, the minister said: "As long as the crossing is operating normally and the facilities [of the crossing] have been repaired."

a2536.speaker: Associated Press (AP)
a2536.speech: Reported that Egypt still has to repair the road crossing the border, which was left full of craters by Israeli air strikes.

a2536.speaker: Khalid Zayed, head of the Red Crescent for North Sinai
a2536.speech: Stressed that more than 200 trucks and around 3,000 tonnes of aid are positioned at or near the Rafah crossing, which is Gaza's only link to Egypt.

a2536.speaker: Joe Biden, US President
a2536.speech: Had previously announced that al-Sissi had agreed to "let up to 20 trucks cross" the border, for the delivery of humanitarian aid to Gaza ; "If Hamas [seizes them] or does not let them through (...) then it will all be over," the US head of state warned ; Biden made the announcement after a telephone conversation with al-Sissi and assured that the Egyptian was "fully cooperative" and that he "deserved a great deal of recognition" for his action.

a2536.speaker: White House officials
a2536.speech: Told the Associated Press (AP) that the aid would go in over the coming days.

a2536.speaker: Israel
a2536.speech: Israel had guaranteed that it would allow Egypt to deliver limited quantities of humanitarian aid to the Gaza Strip, the first concession in a 10-day siege of the territory, provided that these goods do not reach the Palestinian Islamist movement Hamas.

a2536.speaker: UN official for humanitarian emergencies
a2536.speech: Argued on Wednesday that aid to Gaza, once it can cross the Egyptian border, should be "substantial", on the order of 100 trucks per day, and its security assured.

a2536.speaker: Local (Gaza) authorities
a2536.speech: According to local authorities, the Israeli response has caused at least 3,478 deaths in the overcrowded Palestinian territory, most of them civilians.

a2605.speaker: Neal Rijkenberg, Minister of Finance of Eswatini
a2605.speech: Motivating the loan, explained that the government, through EWSC, was implementing a project to expand access to clean water and sanitation for rural households, schools, health centers, and informal settlements; said escalating costs, driven by inflation, exchange rate fluctuations, and unforeseen factors, had created financing shortfalls that require additional resources to complete water supply infrastructure works ; “The loan is highly important to ensure that we drive the agenda of access to clean water. EWSC is better suited to implement the project than any other institution, based on a thorough analysis. The loan will be serviced by the state and will not add to the cost of water for the public.”

a2605.speaker: Neal Rijkenberg, Minister of Finance of Eswatini
a2605.speech: Outlined that the state would repay the loan in 40 semi-annual instalments, beginning after a five-year grace period, with interest at a floating base rate plus a variable spread, a front-end fee of 0.25 per cent of the loan amount, and a commitment charge of 0.25 per cent per annum on the undisbursed balance; acknowledged public frustration over tariffs but insisted that no entity could operate without covering inflation costs, and added that pre-paid meters were already being rolled out, though at a gradual pace.

a2605.speaker: EWSC 2024 annual report
a2605.speech: States that employee benefits expenses rose to E166.9 million from E158.4 million in 2023, an increase of E8.5 million; the cost of corporate gifts surged from E155,198 to E695,312, staff uniforms skyrocketed from E8,309 to E1.4 million, and management car travel expenses totalled E10.3 million; there were 550 employees as of 2024.

a2605.speaker: Manzi Zwane, Nhlambeni MP
a2605.speech: Described EWSC as a ‘monster’ that ordinary people could no longer afford: “Most of the money we pay goes to salaries and luxurious uniforms, even tracksuits. It seems EWSC is now a cash cow, spending willy-nilly on lucrative contracts, while Emaswati struggle with tariffs.”

a2605.speaker: Michael Masilela, Lobamba MP
a2605.speech: Echoed the criticism, saying the corporation appeared to be spending lavishly with little regard for the impoverished: “Tariffs are crippling households and the business community. EWSC must embrace transparency and consider reducing fees, instead of hiking them continuously.”

a2605.speaker: Ntando Mkhonta, Zombodze Emuva MP
a2605.speech: Stressed the importance of improving water connections in Shiselweni and urged colleagues to visit the region to witness the dire need: “Yes, the loan should be approved, but accountability is essential.”

a2605.speaker: Sabelo Mtetwa, Mafutseni MP
a2605.speech: Highlighted governance concerns, urging the minister to ensure competent appointments to parastatal boards: “Cabinet ministers should not appoint their friends to boards. We must have professional oversight. And pre-paid meters should be rolled out faster, so people pay only for what they use.”

a2605.speaker: Mduduzi Dlamini, Nkomiyahlaba MP
a2605.speech: Pressed for a stronger corporate social responsibility drive, criticising the high salaries of senior managers while junior staff faced retrenchments.

a2605.speaker: Sicelo Dlamini, Mayiwane MP
a2605.speech: Dismissed the loan as offside, claiming it would only benefit a few: “EWSC keeps raising tariffs but is not taking money back to the people. Rural water should be prioritised instead.”

a2605.speaker: Sabelo Ndlangamandla, MP
a2605.speech: Opposed the loan, citing exorbitant tariffs and poor infrastructure maintenance: “If pre-paid meters had been fully rolled out, I might support this loan. But as things stand, I cannot.”

a2605.speaker: Thandeka Mavuso, Manzini Region MP
a2605.speech: Questioned how many schools and communities would benefit from the E137.3 million and challenged EWSC to consider public-private partnerships to improve efficiency.

a2605.speaker: Marwick Khumalo, Finance Portfolio Committee Chairperson and Lobamba Lomdzala MP
a2605.speech: Said whether the loan would be approved remained undecided: “Management of EWSC must address the concerns raised by MPs. If approved, it will be tabled in the House on Thursday.”

a2641.speaker: Commercial transport operators – GPRTU of the TUC, GRTCC and other commercial driver groups (joint statement)
a2641.speech: Issued a one-week ultimatum to the Ministry of Roads and Highways to repair the deteriorating Pokuase–Nsawam road or face a mass protest that could ground vehicles; in a joint statement the operators described the stretch as “unmotorable” and “extremely dangerous” to motorists, commuters and residents ; In a statement issued on Thursday, August 14, 2025, the operators noted that the poor condition of the road had rendered it nearly impassable, resulting in increased operational costs due to frequent vehicle maintenance, spare parts replacement, and a reduced vehicle lifespan ; The signatories reiterated “The present deplorable state of the road has made it unmotorable and poses extreme dangers to motorists, commuters and residents along the Pokuase–Nsawam stretch. We are therefore calling on the Hon. Minister of Roads and Highways to take immediate action to fix the Pokuase–Nsawam road to alleviate the plight of motorists, commuters and residents on the corridor. If no meaningful action is taken within one week, the GPRTU of TUC, GRTCC and other commercial transport operators will park our vehicles and embark on a protest against the Government until our concerns are addressed.” ; The unions further called on all motorists, commuters, and residents affected by the situation to join the planned protest as a civic duty to compel the authorities to take action, and stressed that the road’s poor state has not only increased travel time but also imposed heavy operational costs on drivers.

a2641.speaker: Transport unions (GPRTU, GRTCC and others)
a2641.speech: According to the unions, the Minister for Roads and Highways, Kwame Governs Agbodza, had earlier assured them that the road would be put in satisfactory condition within six weeks, but the deadline had long passed without any improvement.

a2641.speaker: Several frustrated drivers
a2641.speech: Appealed to the government to release funds for the contractor to resume work.

a2641.speaker: Philip Mensah, articulated truck driver transporting cement
a2641.speech: Lamented: “I have never slept on this section of the road before, but here I am. I have to deliver this consignment before the end of the day, and look, I am stuck in the middle of the road.”

a2641.speaker: Michael Ansah, fuel tanker driver
a2641.speech: Expressed concern for his safety: “I am worried because the product I am carrying is flammable and can catch fire easily.”

a2641.speaker: Evans Appiah, driver transporting perishable goods
a2641.speech: Feared his consignment would go to waste: “The products need refrigeration, and any delay will spoil them. The government must pay the contractor so work can continue.”

a2641.speaker: Emmanuel Ofori, taxi driver
a2641.speech: Recounted how a routine trip turned into a nightmare: “I was just dropping a customer at Medie, only to pass the night on the road.”

a2641.speaker: Kwame Governs Agbodza, Minister for Roads and Highways
a2641.speech: Has previously expressed dissatisfaction with the slow progress of work, acknowledging financial constraints but urging contractors to expedite delivery given the strategic importance of the corridor; has reiterated the government’s commitment to completing all ongoing road projects, including the Ofankor–Nsawam stretch ; Speaking to journalists during an inspection tour, he said: “I acknowledge that the majority of road contractors are having a crisis of not being paid because the volume of work that had been awarded without any sustainable source of funding is the issue. That is the bottom line.” He added: “I agree every road is necessary, every single road that is under contract is necessary, but you know the corridor you are working on is a very critical one. You have to actually increase your activity on this corridor in good faith because surely we owe, and you will be paid.”

a2641.speaker: Mahama Abdulai, Project Manager for the Ofankor–Nsawam project
a2641.speech: Has attributed the slowdown in work to litigation, compensation issues and financial constraints, and has appealed to the Minister for urgent intervention.

a2641.speaker: Other reports (cited)
a2641.speech: Have quoted a figure of US$346.5 million for the project, which is funded by the Government of Ghana at GH¢341.48 million.

a2893.speaker: Corporate Council on Africa (CCA)
a2893.speech: Has called for the urgent renewal of two cornerstone United States policy instruments, the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) and the International Development Finance Corporation (DFC), warning that delays could stall progress in strengthening trade and investment ties with Africa.

a2893.speaker: Florizelle Liser, president and Chief Executive Officer of the Corporate Council on Africa
a2893.speech: Said both programmes, which lapsed earlier this month, were critical to maintaining investor confidence and advancing Africa's integration into global markets ; “AGOA and DFC are two main policy areas on the U.S. side that we need to get focused on if we're going to make sure that Africa can trade more with a large market like the United States,” Ms Liser said. “Despite existing tariffs, duty-free access to the U.S. market remains very important. We need AGOA reauthorised, and we need DFC reauthorised so that it can support the kind of investments U.S. companies are already making and would like to do in Africa.”

a2893.speaker: Florizelle Liser, president and CEO of the Corporate Council on Africa
a2893.speech: Highlighted the role of the Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC), which has invested over US$10 billion in African infrastructure over the past 20 years: “In the last two decades, the MCC has invested over $10 billion in Africa, mainly in infrastructure,” she said. “A lot of people don't realise this. While China is often cited as the dominant player, the United States and other partners have also been making significant, long-term investments that are transforming communities and strengthening trade connectivity.”

a2893.speaker: Florizelle Liser, president and CEO of the Corporate Council on Africa
a2893.speech: Said such investments are vital to realizing the goals of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) by improving regional integration and cross-border connectivity: “For U.S. investors to come to Africa, they need larger markets and regional integration,” she explained. “The AfCFTA is being implemented, and trade among Africans is happening – but not yet at the scale it needs to be. Infrastructure is the key to unlocking that growth.”

a2893.speaker: Florizelle Liser, president and CEO of the Corporate Council on Africa
a2893.speech: Stressed that the lack of coordinated cross-border infrastructure and fragmented regulatory frameworks continues to deter investors and delay project implementation: “Many infrastructure projects stop at the borders because they are planned nationally, not regionally,” Ms. Liser observed. “To move faster, governments and development finance institutions need to harmonise standards, streamline procurement, and strengthen institutional capacity.”

a2893.speaker: Florizelle Liser, president and CEO of the Corporate Council on Africa
a2893.speech: Added that reliable energy access remains one of the most pressing challenges for African industry and competitiveness: “I have not been to one factory in Africa that did not rely on a generator,” she noted. “That alone shows how crucial energy and power infrastructure are for productivity and trade.”

a2909.speaker: Mo Ali, Managing Director of the Liberia Water and Sewer Corporation (LWSC)
a2909.speech: “That crowning achievement for me will be to reach water supply to all the 15 county capitals, and also reach water supply to big towns like Ganta, Karnplay, and other places; but first, the first capitals. Pleebo, like Bopolu, has never had water supply and that is the most populated city in the Southeast. We are going to carry water there. Next year, we will consider other places. For me, the crowning moment will be for the county capitals and bigger cities to get water supply.”

a2909.speaker: Mo Ali, Managing Director of the LWSC
a2909.speech: Admitted that the LWSC under his helm has not reached the turning point, yet it has started the journey of recovery: “I think it’s the start of a very long journey. The entity was established in 1973 to provide water and sewerage services for Monrovia, the county capitals, and communities that have populations of 5,000 and above. The structure that we have today was constructed in 1953, and the LWSC for the wrong reasons had been underperforming. We don’t like to blame anyone, but we thought they were management issues. We are not getting extra support, but we believe that the collective effort that we’re making to transform the institution is starting a revolution at the entity.”

a2909.speaker: Mo Ali, Managing Director of the LWSC
a2909.speech: Said the Bopolu Water Station project was conceived by Gbarpolu County Senator Amara Konneh who approached the LWSC and said the city has never got a running water supply: “For the most part, the people there draw water from creeks, wells or hand pumps. And so, he pleaded with the LWSC and then we all lobbied with the Ministry of Finance and the Legislature to make budgetary allocation for the project there. The initial thought was that we would have got US$500,000 to run the pipe through the entire town... We got US$250,000, and then we sent out the bid and contractors came in. Eventually, Tenda... was selected based on their experience and their efficiency in working. So, they constructed the water project. The people there are excited because there are several things that come with water being on the premises or easily accessible... The second thing is it also helps to reduce the spread of water-borne diseases like diarrhea and other things.”

a2909.speaker: Amara Konneh, Gbarpolu County Senator (as reported by Mo Ali)
a2909.speech: Approached the LWSC and said the city has never got a running water supply, and pleaded with the LWSC to bring a water project to Bopolu.

a2909.speaker: Mo Ali, Managing Director of the LWSC
a2909.speech: Said the people of Gbarpolu or Bopolu deserve development just like others in any part of the country and defended the US$250,000 price tag: “Maybe they believe that the people of Gbarpolu or Bopolu do not deserve to have good water supply, but we don’t think that way. We believe that everywhere in this place deserves a better, clean water supply... The price tag, anybody who says the cost is high does not understand what we mean when we say a pipe network is laid in a community... The length of that 4-inch pipe is above 1.7 kilometers. Then we also have the secondary transmission line which is a 2-inch pipe that is around 1.3 kilometers. Then we have the tertiary transmission line... a ¾-inch pipe, and that is around 239 meters... It is powered by a solar system. Besides that, the materials that were used in the majority of them were imported because it’s not just the ordinary pipe that they sell in the stores. Those pipes are meant to last for decades... but it involves labor cost. You’re digging more than 3 kilometers of ground to lay pipe, we didn’t carry machines to dig it. The company hired people from right there.”

a2909.speaker: Mo Ali, Managing Director of the LWSC
a2909.speech: Admitted that initially they had thought to extend pipe water to five counties this year: “We had a negotiation with USAID where we did a complete engineering feasibility on the water system in Kakata and that of Buchanan. We have signed an agreement. By now, the construction and rehabilitation should have begun. But then we had the unfortunate work stop which has greatly affected us in a negative sense. But we will still move forward. The one with Zwedru, Pleebo, and Greenville, they are still on course. They are sending out bids to companies that should participate in the bidding process... So, we are on course with those three... In Zwedru and Greenville, we will be rehabilitating. So, Greenville has been down since the early 90s during the civil crisis; and Zwedru was rehabilitated but then they went back down due to management issues and finances in 2019. We will be rehabilitating those two and constructing new systems.”

a2909.speaker: Mo Ali, Managing Director of the LWSC
a2909.speech: Said the first thing is that almost everybody thinks that water should be free: “And it is that mindset that people go with that makes them not pay water bills... We use seven to nine million United States dollars’ worth of electricity every year at the White Plains... We use chemicals to purify the water, three different chemicals, very expensive... We use pretty close to sixty to seventy thousand dollars’ worth of chemicals every month to purify the water... So, what are we doing for sustainability? We have outsourced our Sanniquellie water system to a private contractor, and they have introduced the prepayment. Just within the 50 customers that have been issued prepaid meters, the revenue among those 50 customers has jumped from $300 to $2,000. We have now concluded with our Board of Directors that we will pilot the prepaid meters in Monrovia and Paynesville... This time around, once we start the prepaid meter, you will only use what you pay... Also, when we introduce that, we will have water vending points in communities that you can just walk to and pay for your water.”

a2909.speaker: Mo Ali, Managing Director of the LWSC
a2909.speech: Said one of the first things his administration did was to draft and complete the workers’ manual, the HR and policy manual: “And then we reprogrammed the organogram of the institution that tells us exactly how many employees that we need... It is not intended to target anyone. But one of the reasons why I came here is to make the system efficient and effective. And being efficient does not mean you must be overstaffed... The payroll when I took over at LWSC was between three hundred and eighty to three hundred and eight-two thousand United States Dollars every month. The entity is generating less than two hundred thousand dollars a month. So, you can see that we have to beg the Finance Ministry every month for money to pay the employees. The introduction of prepaid meters will eliminate the needs for meter readers... We are also going to see if the technology can detect water leaks because that’s one of our major challenges. We lose a lot of water to leakage, more than 50 percent of what is pumped from White Plains goes through theft and leaks; and you have 25% going towards unpaid bills. In our studies, non-revenue water accounts for 60-70% of whatever we produce from White Plains.”

a2909.speaker: Mo Ali, Managing Director of the LWSC
a2909.speech: Said credibility is a critical issue and does not only deal with international partners but local vendors as well: “As it stands, no local vendor credits Water and Sewer... because Water and Sewer owes almost everyone, and every day we are in court. And that’s not good for the entity’s credibility... With the international partners, the donors, what we have to do is to ensure that we have projects with them... we asked for another year’s extension. The World Bank granted that. The project is now on course; 10 kilometers of 48-inch pipes that should be replacing the current 36-inch pipe that supplies Monrovia should be arriving in the country on March 15... So, the way to increase confidence and credibility is to implement as agreed between LWSC and donors... Also, live by the terms. Account for whatever they give you. So, one of the things that we’ve done when we took over is to call for an audit for the last three years which the GAC has completed... the GAC will be doing audits every year as long as I am here. Those audit reports will be published so that partners can see, and Liberians can see. I believe that is the most efficient way of building the credibility of the entity.”

a2909.speaker: World Bank (as reported by Mo Ali)
a2909.speech: Said this is the last time we are going to talk about this project, and that if the LWSC cannot get it on track it will withdraw the funding; granted the requested one-year extension.

a2909.speaker: Mo Ali, Managing Director of the LWSC
a2909.speech: Said the transition from politics to public service comes with the territory, and that he expects people to criticize him for personal and institutional growth: “Last night I was reading a profile, and they said in it, flowers require sun and rain to grow. As humans and politicians, we need both criticisms and praise to improve ourselves. If everybody is just praising you, you’re bound to fall and make mistakes. For us, we welcome the criticisms... it only teaches me that when you criticize other people and you are given the opportunity to serve, make sure to do it properly because there will be so many eyes on you. And I can understand the level of critique I go under probably more than any other government official, but I understand that and I like it because it is a challenge to me... So, for me, I welcome the criticism because it’s going to help improve our working environment and help us succeed at Water and Sewer.”

a3198.speaker: Ethiopia (presentation at the Second Africa Climate Summit)
a3198.speech: Boldly presented the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) as a powerful example of a homegrown, African-led solution to the climate crisis, and underscored a key message of the summit: that a self-determined approach to development is essential for achieving a sustainable and prosperous future for the continent.

a3198.speaker: Ethiopian officials, including Fitsum Assefa, Minister of Planning and Development
a3198.speech: Championed the GERD as a cornerstone of the nation's proactive climate strategy.

a3502.speaker: World Health Organisation (WHO) report
a3502.speech: Has raised concerns over major disruptions in health services across the world, noting that 70 per cent of its country offices have observed major impacts caused by recent donor funding cuts; attributed the disruptions to the sudden suspension and reduction of Official Development Assistance (ODA) for health; said the findings are based on a rapid assessment carried out in March and April 2025 across 108 WHO country offices, primarily located in lower-middle-income countries; emphasised that the current situation poses serious threats to the functioning of global health systems and demands immediate international attention.

a3502.speaker: World Health Organisation (WHO) report
a3502.speech: Reported that the suspensions and reductions in ODA are disrupting all health system functions, with the most frequently reported impacts being on health emergency preparedness and response (70 per cent), public health surveillance (66 per cent), service provision (58 per cent), humanitarian aid (56 per cent), and the health and care workforce (54 per cent); noted that the cuts are already forcing people to pay more out-of-pocket for healthcare in some countries, with about 24 per cent of responses indicating that budget constraints are pushing costs directly onto patients, especially the poor and vulnerable. "The pause in ODA has led to job losses for health and care workers in over half of responding countries and significant disruptions to trainings. Information systems are particularly impacted as key health data collection is disrupted. Over 40 per cent of countries experienced disruptions to key information systems, including collaborative surveillance and emergency systems, health management information systems, disease-specific reporting systems, lab information systems, and household/population surveys."

a3502.speaker: World Health Organisation (WHO)
a3502.speech: Noted that it will continue to monitor the situation closely and work with donor agencies and health partners to design and implement urgent response plans; warned that unless urgent steps are taken, the ripple effects of the funding crisis could be long-lasting and devastating.

a3502.speaker: Recent UN report
a3502.speech: Warned that recent cuts to global health aid could reverse progress in reducing maternal deaths.

a3502.speaker: Tedros Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General
a3502.speech: Described the results as alarming and called for an accelerated transition to sustainable domestic funding; said these results show the impact of the sudden and unplanned cuts to aid on the health of millions of people. "Although these cuts are a shock, they are also driving an accelerated transition away from aid dependency to a more sustainable self-reliance, based on domestic resources." ; "Many countries are asking for WHO's support, and WHO is working with them to identify and tailor the most effective measures."

a3614.speaker: Johnson Kuol Gai, Commissioner of Fangak County, Jonglei State
a3614.speech: Appealed for urgent humanitarian assistance for flood-affected communities, citing severe shortages of food, shelter, and medical services: “The community of Fangak is really suffering. The area is submerged. They have no food, no shelter, and not even a clinic. I’m appealing to all agencies operating in South Sudan to come and witness this situation.” ; Added that due to poor network coverage, many displaced residents were unaware of the visit and could not gather at the administrative centre, and emphasized the community’s commitment to peace but stressed that basic humanitarian needs must be addressed.

a3614.speaker: General Kong Thuo, Assistant Chief of Defence Forces for Operations
a3614.speech: Urged residents and organized forces to support peace efforts during a visit to assess the security situation in the area.

a4086.speaker: Jose Maria Neves, President of Cabo Verde
a4086.speech: Speaking at the reception of the Government's New Year greetings, stressed that the gains achieved in the past year are important for Cape Verde and help project the image of a country with a functioning democratic rule of law, a country committed to building factors of competitiveness and to ensuring that all its citizens live with dignity. "First of all, I highlight the fact that the country has secured a third Millennium Challenge Account compact. This is a gain that results from Cape Verde's good performance in areas that are essential for our future. I am referring to good governance, investment in people, and the creation of conditions for us to be a far more competitive economy, with inclusive and environmentally sustainable growth." ; Also highlighted the fact that Cape Verde may obtain certification as a malaria-free country, stressing that this gain shows the country's progress, the investments made in the health sector and the commitment of all the authorities and of civil society; and referred to 2024 having been proclaimed by the Government as the year of mental health, stressing the importance of mobilising resources through public-private partnerships to tackle mental illness in Cape Verde.

a4086.speaker: Jose Maria Neves, President of Cabo Verde
a4086.speech: Underlined that the country entered 2024 with many challenges, starting with those resulting from the impacts of wars and conflicts on the international stage on the Cape Verdean economic fabric and on the diaspora, and argued that it is necessary to keep working. "We have to do everything to speed up the pace. Those who have difficulty finding work, those who still live in extreme poverty, those who have difficulty accessing health services, or transport services, or education services, are in a hurry, and we necessarily have to speed up the pace so that people can face, with much more success, the problems that still exist." ; Wished the Government a good year and success, stressing that the Government's success is Cape Verde's success.

a4086.speaker: Ulisses Correia e Silva, Prime Minister of Cabo Verde
a4086.speech: Said that even in the face of great challenges there are hopes and new expectations, and so he hopes that 2024 will be a year of achievement. "We have a context that is still very difficult, an external context that makes the year very demanding. Risks, uncertainties, the wars that affect the world economies and our economy. And in Cape Verde we are committed to continuing to fight the good fights, in order to be more resilient. We have a strong commitment to increasing employment, reducing poverty, and economic growth, so that we can move forward within this difficult context." ; Said he hoped for "a good complementarity of powers", namely of the Government, Parliament and the Presidency of the Republic, so that together they can help the country get through these very demanding times.
